summary: Illustrative example: smaller photographs could upload faster, but quality has not been established. No deployment is authorized.
prompt_verbatim: Show a newcomer what we tried, why we tried it, what we learned and what should happen next.

changes.title: From a size idea to a testable speed-and-quality question
changes.before: Large photos take longer to send, but changing the encoder has not been tested.
changes.after: The proposed comparison keeps the photographs fixed and checks speed and visual detail separately; no experiment has run.
changes.why_it_matters: The next decision needs both transfer and quality evidence, not simply a smaller-file example.

limitations.question: Will smaller files preserve detail on new photographs?
limitations.why_unanswered: The attached numbers illustrate report formatting, not measured speed or quality.
limitations.goal_impact: A faster upload would not meet the goal if photographs lost visible detail.
limitations.next_evidence: A separately approved complete comparison on held-out photos with a fixed quality assessment.

insights.title: Why the example is not a product result
insights.comparison: The intended study compares two encoders on identical public photographs under fixed upload settings.
insights.support: Zero measured photographs: the attached report is explicitly illustrative.
insights.finding: No speed or visual-quality outcome has been collected.
insights.interpretation: The example demonstrates how to explain a study, not that an encoder improves the product.
insights.goal_relevance: Prepare a quality-and-speed decision before deployment instead of optimizing file size alone.
insights.caveat: No claim about unseen photographs or production upload performance is supported.

workflow.goal: Upload photographs faster without losing visible detail.
workflow.background: Large image files take longer to send. This example explains how a research team could compare smaller image encodings before changing the product. Its numbers are illustrative, not measured evidence.
success_criteria: Independent image-quality checks must pass before any deployment.
workflow.current_question: Can a different image encoding reduce file size without reducing quality?
workflow.next_checkpoint: Collect a complete speed and quality comparison under a separately approved experiment contract.

glossary.meaning: A method used to encode or compress an image.
Old transfer time divided by new transfer time; 1.2 would mean 20% more work per unit time, not proven here.

efforts.title: Explore a more compact image encoding
efforts.question: Would smaller files reduce transfer time?
efforts.motivation: File size is a direct, controllable input to transfer time.
efforts.approach: Compare two encoders on identical public photographs; check speed and image quality separately.

alternatives.reason: It changes infrastructure and would not isolate the encoding effect.

efforts.outcome: No experiment has been run. The attached illustrative report only demonstrates the review format.
efforts.decision: Do not deploy; prepare a complete comparison first.
efforts.rationale: A smaller file is useful only if it preserves acceptable image quality.
efforts.uncertainty: Quality of unseen photographs is untested, and the illustrative speedup is not a measurement.
efforts.next_step: Freeze the image selection, quality verifier and complete-unit experiment budget.
